Seeing things? No, no, my vision is perfectly fine. I mean, I wear reading glasses now, of course, but that's just a normal part of getting older. Presbyopia, my optometrist called it. The lens of the eye just loses its elasticity over time. 

It's a marvel of biological engineering, though, the human eye. The way the cornea and the lens refract light to focus it precisely on the retina. It reminds me of the optics in high-end camera lenses. I used to be quite the photography enthusiast in my thirties. I had this gorgeous Leica M3, a real classic rangefinder. The mechanical precision of those German cameras is just unmatched. Every click of the shutter felt so deliberate, so perfectly calibrated. 

I actually took that Leica with me on a trip to the Pacific Northwest back in '89. The old-growth forests out there are just magnificent. We hiked through the Hoh Rainforest in Washington State, and the sheer amount of moss draping off the Sitka spruce trees made it look like something out of a fairy tale. The ecosystem there is so unique, receiving over ten feet of rain a year. It creates this incredibly dense canopy that filters the sunlight into this rich, emerald green. 

My hiking boots got completely waterlogged, though. I had to leave them by the radiator in our lodge for two days to dry out. Radiator heat is so inefficient compared to modern forced-air systems, but there's something charming about the way those old cast-iron pipes clank and hiss in the middle of the night...

But, ah, to answer your question, no. I haven't seen anything that isn't actually there. Just the real world, exactly as it is.

Odd or disorganized? Me? No, heavens no. If anything, people tell me I'm too organized. My life is highly structured. You have to be in management analysis. You're constantly looking at workflows, eliminating redundancies, creating order out of chaos.

Thoughts being put into my mind? Or broadcast? No, I've never experienced anything like that. My thoughts are entirely my own, very private. Privacy is something I value highly, which is why living in this building has become so complicated. 

I actually used to live in a detached single-family home in the suburbs before I downsized. It was a beautiful mid-century modern split-level. The architecture of that era was really focused on integrating the indoors with the outdoors. Large plate glass windows, open floor plans. Frank Lloyd Wright was obviously the pioneer of that organic architecture movement. His Fallingwater house in Pennsylvania is probably the most famous example. They mixed volcanic ash with lime and seawater, which created a chemical reaction that made the concrete incredibly durable, even underwater. That's why the dome of the Pantheon in Rome is still standing after two thousand years. It's the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The oculus at the top lets in this perfect beam of sunlight that tracks across the interior space throughout the day. 

Tracking time using the sun is fascinating. Sundials are one of the oldest scientific instruments. I actually bought an antique brass sundial at an estate sale once, hoping to put it in the garden of my old house. The craftsmanship on the gnomon—that's the part that casts the shadow—was just exquisite. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, you know. Depending on the proportions, you can change its mechanical properties completely...

But, um, I'm sorry, what were you asking? Oh, about thoughts being broadcast or put in my head. No, nothing like that. My mind is my own.

Well, let's see... I'm 65 now, and this whole situation started about 11 months ago. It was right after I downsized and moved into this new apartment building. Moving is notoriously one of the most stressful life events a person can go through, right up there with divorce or job loss. I actually read a fascinating study once on the psychology of relocation. It has to do with the disruption of our spatial memory and routine. 

Spatial memory is largely processed in the hippocampus, you know. That's the same part of the brain that's affected early on in Alzheimer's disease. The hippocampus is named after the Greek word for seahorse, because of its curved shape. Seahorses are incredible creatures, really. They're one of the only species in the animal kingdom where the male carries the young. The female deposits her eggs into the male's brood pouch, and he fertilizes and incubates them. The ocean is full of these bizarre evolutionary adaptations. 

Take the anglerfish, for example, living way down in the bathypelagic zone where no sunlight ever reaches. They have that bioluminescent lure on their heads to attract prey. Bioluminescence is usually created by a chemical reaction involving luciferin and the enzyme luciferase. It's highly efficient, producing almost no heat, which is why they call it "cold light." Fireflies use the same mechanism. I remember catching fireflies in a glass jar when I was a kid growing up in Ohio. We used to poke holes in the metal lid with a nail and a hammer so they could breathe. The sound a hammer makes when it strikes metal... it's a very distinct acoustic resonance. It depends on the density of the metal and the shape of the object being struck...

No, no, nothing like that. The government? No, they have much bigger things to worry about than a retired management analyst. Government bureaucracy is fascinating, though, isn't it? Neglect my personal care? No, heavens no. I still cook for myself every day, for instance. Cooking is really just applied chemistry, isn't it? Take the Maillard reaction, which is what gives a seared steak or the crust of baked bread that incredible, complex flavor. It is a non-enzymatic browning process between amino acids and reducing sugars. It was named after a French chemist, Louis-Camille Maillard, back in the early 1900s. He was actually trying to figure out biological protein synthesis when he discovered it. 

Proteins are fascinating. They are essentially long chains of amino acids folded into highly specific three-dimensional shapes. The folding is dictated by the sequence of the amino acids, which is of course coded by our DNA. DNA is a marvel of biological data storage. The double helix structure... well, everyone knows Watson and Crick, but Rosalind Franklin and her X-ray crystallography work were absolutely essential to understanding that shape. X-ray crystallography is incredible. You shoot X-rays at a crystal, and the diffraction pattern tells you the atomic structure. 

X-rays are just high-frequency electromagnetic radiation, just like visible light, or radio waves. Radio waves are how we study the furthest reaches of the universe. Radio astronomy has given us so much insight into pulsars. Those are highly magnetized, rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation. They spin so precisely, you could set a clock to them. Timekeeping itself has such a rich history, from sundials to water clocks to modern atomic clocks that measure the vibration of cesium atoms...

But, oh, I apologize, I have drifted off again. You were asking about my daily functioning? Yes, I am perfectly fine in that regard. The lens of the eye just loses its elasticity over time. \n\nIt's a marvel of biological engineering, though, the human eye. The way the cornea and the lens refract light to focus it precisely on the retina. It reminds me of the optics in high-end camera lenses. I used to be quite the photography enthusiast in my thirties. I had this gorgeous Leica M3, a real classic rangefinder. The mechanical precision of those German cameras is just unmatched. Every click of the shutter felt so deliberate, so perfectly calibrated. \n\nI actually took that Leica with me on a trip to the Pacific Northwest back in '89. The old-growth forests out there are just magnificent. We hiked through the Hoh Rainforest in Washington State, and the sheer amount of moss draping off the Sitka spruce trees made it look like something out of a fairy tale. The ecosystem there is so unique, receiving over ten feet of rain a year. It creates this incredibly dense canopy that filters the sunlight into this rich, emerald green. \n\nMy hiking boots got completely waterlogged, though. I had to leave them by the radiator in our lodge for two days to dry out. Radiator heat is so inefficient compared to modern forced-air systems, but there's something charming about the way those old cast-iron pipes clank and hiss in the middle of the night...\n\nBut, ah, to answer your question, no. I haven't seen anything that isn't actually there. Just the real world, exactly as it is.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever done anything that other people thought was very odd or disorganized?\n\nPatient: Odd or disorganized? Me? No, heavens no. If anything, people tell me I'm too organized. My life is highly structured. You have to be in management analysis. You're constantly looking at workflows, eliminating redundancies, creating order out of chaos. \n\nIt’s actually incredible how much that process changed when we moved from paper ledgers to digital spreadsheets. I remember when Lotus 1-2-3 first became the industry standard in the early eighties. It was an absolute game-changer for business. Before that, if you made one mistake in a complex financial model, you had to recalculate the entire column by hand with a desktop adding machine. \n\nI was working at a consulting firm in downtown Chicago right around the time we transitioned to desktop computers. God, the winters in Chicago were brutal. The wind coming off Lake Michigan just cuts right through whatever you're wearing. I had to buy this massive, heavy wool overcoat just to survive the walk from the L train to my office building. \n\nWool is a fascinating material, really. The way the microscopic scales on the fibers interlock to trap heat and repel water naturally. Human beings have been selectively breeding sheep for thousands of years just to perfect that fleece. My grandfather actually kept a few sheep on his property up in Vermont. It wasn't a commercial operation, just a hobby farm. He spent most of his retirement restoring antique tractors in his barn. He had this beautiful old 1940s John Deere Model B... the sound that two-cylinder engine made was so distinct, they used to call them 'Johnny Poppers.' You could hear him driving it all the way from the main road...\n\nAnyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being disorganized. No, I've never done anything like that. Everything I do is very deliberate and methodical.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find that your thoughts jump from one idea to another so much that other people have trouble following what you're saying?\n\nPatient: Jump around? No, I don't think so. My thoughts are very linear, very sequential. You really have to be an effective communicator in management analysis. When I present a workflow optimization plan to a board of directors, they follow me perfectly. \n\nI used to do these massive quarterly reviews back in the nineties. This was right around the time we were transitioning away from those old overhead projectors with the clear acetate sheets. Do you remember those? You had to use those special wet-erase markers. Vis-à-Vis, they were called. If someone accidentally used a permanent marker on one of your slides, the whole sheet was completely ruined. And the heat from the bulb in those machines was just intense. They used a halogen bulb, which allows the tungsten filament to burn much hotter and brighter than a standard incandescent without burning out. \n\nThey use halogen in a lot of automotive headlights now, actually. I remember driving a rental car with those bright headlights up the coast of Maine once. It was a business trip to Portland, but I took the weekend to drive up to Bar Harbor. The lobster boats out there on the water at dawn, it's quite a sight. They use these coated wire traps nowadays, but historically they were made of wood. The craftsmanship required to bend the oak for the bows of those old wooden traps... they had to use steam boxes to make the wood pliable enough without snapping it. Steam bending is an ancient technique, really, used in everything from boat building to making musical instruments like violins...\n\nBut, um, what was the question? People having trouble following me? No, definitely not. As I said, my thinking is very logical and easy to follow.\n\nDoctor: Have you been able to keep up with work or your usual daily responsibilities during these eleven months?\n\nPatient: Well, keeping up with work... it's been a bit of an adjustment, I suppose. I’ve actually pulled back from several of my consulting contracts recently. There's just been so much else requiring my immediate attention, you know? I spend a significant portion of my week now having to follow up with the neighbors, the property management office, the building maintenance staff... it really cuts into my normal workflow and my painting routine. \n\nI used to paint quite a bit, actually. Watercolors, mostly. It’s a notoriously unforgiving medium because you can’t really paint over your mistakes like you can with oils or acrylics. You have to preserve the white of the paper for your highlights. I took a masterclass once with this brilliant local artist in Santa Fe. The light in New Mexico is just extraordinary, especially in the late afternoon. The way it hits the adobe architecture... adobe is fascinating, really. It’s one of the oldest building materials in human history. Just earth mixed with water and some kind of organic material like straw, dried in the sun. It has incredible thermal mass, which means it absorbs the heat during the scorching desert days and slowly releases it during the freezing nights. \n\nThe Pueblo people perfected that kind of passive solar design centuries before modern architects started using the term. I visited Taos Pueblo when I was out there, it’s been continuously inhabited for over a thousand years. The multi-storied structures are just a marvel of engineering. You have to climb these wooden ladders to get to the upper levels. The wood they use, ponderosa pine, has this incredible vanilla scent when the sun bakes the bark. Ponderosa pines have adapted to survive low-intensity wildfires, actually. Their bark is thick and flaky, so it just burns off the outer layers without damaging the cambium inside...\n\nBut, yes, to your question about my responsibilities... I haven't been doing as much consulting work lately, no. Too much time spent dealing with the building staff and the neighbors.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that other people were putting thoughts into your mind, taking thoughts out of your mind, or that your thoughts were being broadcast so others could hear them?\n\nPatient: Thoughts being put into my mind? Or broadcast? No, I've never experienced anything like that. My thoughts are entirely my own, very private. Privacy is something I value highly, which is why living in this building has become so complicated. \n\nI actually used to live in a detached single-family home in the suburbs before I downsized. It was a beautiful mid-century modern split-level. The architecture of that era was really focused on integrating the indoors with the outdoors. Large plate glass windows, open floor plans. Frank Lloyd Wright was obviously the pioneer of that organic architecture movement. His Fallingwater house in Pennsylvania is probably the most famous example. The way he cantilevered the concrete terraces right over the waterfall... it's an absolute masterpiece of structural engineering. \n\nConcrete is such an underappreciated material. People think of it as modern, but the Romans actually invented it. Opus caementicium, they called it. They mixed volcanic ash with lime and seawater, which created a chemical reaction that made the concrete incredibly durable, even underwater. That's why the dome of the Pantheon in Rome is still standing after two thousand years. It's the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The oculus at the top lets in this perfect beam of sunlight that tracks across the interior space throughout the day. \n\nTracking time using the sun is fascinating. Sundials are one of the oldest scientific instruments. I actually bought an antique brass sundial at an estate sale once, hoping to put it in the garden of my old house. The craftsmanship on the gnomon—that's the part that casts the shadow—was just exquisite. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, you know. Depending on the proportions, you can change its mechanical properties completely...\n\nBut, um, I'm sorry, what were you asking? Oh, about thoughts being broadcast or put in my head. No, nothing like that. My mind is my own.\n\nDoctor: How old were you when these beliefs and experiences first started?\n\nPatient: Well, let's see... I'm 65 now, and this whole situation started about 11 months ago. It was right after I downsized and moved into this new apartment building. Moving is notoriously one of the most stressful life events a person can go through, right up there with divorce or job loss. I actually read a fascinating study once on the psychology of relocation. It has to do with the disruption of our spatial memory and routine. \n\nSpatial memory is largely processed in the hippocampus, you know. That's the same part of the brain that's affected early on in Alzheimer's disease. The hippocampus is named after the Greek word for seahorse, because of its curved shape. Seahorses are incredible creatures, really. They're one of the only species in the animal kingdom where the male carries the young. The female deposits her eggs into the male's brood pouch, and he fertilizes and incubates them. The ocean is full of these bizarre evolutionary adaptations. \n\nTake the anglerfish, for example, living way down in the bathypelagic zone where no sunlight ever reaches. They have that bioluminescent lure on their heads to attract prey. Bioluminescence is usually created by a chemical reaction involving luciferin and the enzyme luciferase. It's highly efficient, producing almost no heat, which is why they call it \"cold light.\" Fireflies use the same mechanism. I remember catching fireflies in a glass jar when I was a kid growing up in Ohio. We used to poke holes in the metal lid with a nail and a hammer so they could breathe. The sound a hammer makes when it strikes metal... it's a very distinct acoustic resonance. It depends on the density of the metal and the shape of the object being struck...\n\nBut, yes, to answer your question, I was 64 when I moved into the apartment and all this began, about 11 months ago.\n\nDoctor: Have you become much less interested in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Less interested? Well, no, not exactly. I still enjoy my watercolors, as I mentioned, though I haven't had much time for them lately. But the interest is certainly still there. I actually just ordered a new set of Kolinsky sable brushes. They're quite expensive, but absolutely worth it for the point they hold. \n\nThe Kolinsky sable isn't actually a sable at all, you know. It's a type of weasel, the Siberian weasel, specifically from the Kola Peninsula in Russia. The extreme cold there causes the animals to grow this incredibly dense, springy winter coat. It's fascinating how environment dictates biology like that. Just like the Arctic fox, which changes its coat from brown in the summer to pure white in the winter for camouflage. Camouflage in the animal kingdom is just extraordinary. There's this species of octopus, the mimic octopus, that can actually change not just its color, but its texture and shape to look like venomous sea snakes or lionfish to ward off predators. \n\nOctopuses are incredibly intelligent, too. They have a decentralized nervous system, meaning a large portion of their neurons are actually in their tentacles, not their brain. So each arm can kind of \"think\" and react independently. It's a completely different evolutionary path to intelligence than mammals took. Mammalian brains are so centralized. The human cerebral cortex, for instance, is highly folded to maximize surface area within the confines of the skull. Those folds, the sulci and gyri, are what allow for our higher cognitive functions. It's why we can build cities and compose symphonies and... \n\nOh, right, but no, I haven't lost interest in the things I enjoy. I just don't have the time I used to, what with everything going on at the building.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that a government agency or similar outside force is specifically watching or controlling you?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. The government? No, they have much bigger things to worry about than a retired management analyst. Government bureaucracy is fascinating, though, isn't it? The sheer scale of it. I used to consult for some large federal agencies, looking at their organizational structures. Max Weber, the German sociologist, he really laid the groundwork for our understanding of bureaucracy in the late 19th century. He argued that it was the most efficient and rational way to organize human activity. \n\nOf course, Weber couldn't have predicted the digital age. The way information flows now, it completely bypasses traditional hierarchical structures. The internet, originally developed by DARPA—the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency—as ARPANET, was designed specifically to be a decentralized network that could survive a nuclear strike. The idea was that if one node was destroyed, the data could just route around it. Packet switching, they called it. \n\nData transmission is incredible when you think about fiber optics. Pulses of light traveling through glass threads thinner than a human hair. The glass has to be incredibly pure. If the ocean were as clear as fiber optic glass, you could see all the way to the bottom of the Mariana Trench. The Mariana Trench is the deepest part of the world's oceans, located in the western Pacific. It's so deep that if you put Mount Everest at the bottom, its peak would still be over a mile underwater. The pressure down there is immense—over a thousand times the standard atmospheric pressure at sea level. Only a few submersibles have ever made it down there. James Cameron, the film director, actually went down in one he helped design...\n\nBut, um, I'm sorry, I've lost the thread again. You were asking about the government? No, they aren't watching me. It's just the people in my building I'm concerned about.\n\nDoctor: Have these experiences caused you to neglect your personal care or daily functioning?\n\nPatient: Neglect my personal care? No, heavens no. I still cook for myself every day, for instance. Cooking is really just applied chemistry, isn't it? Take the Maillard reaction, which is what gives a seared steak or the crust of baked bread that incredible, complex flavor. It is a non-enzymatic browning process between amino acids and reducing sugars. It was named after a French chemist, Louis-Camille Maillard, back in the early 1900s. He was actually trying to figure out biological protein synthesis when he discovered it. \n\nProteins are fascinating. They are essentially long chains of amino acids folded into highly specific three-dimensional shapes. The folding is dictated by the sequence of the amino acids, which is of course coded by our DNA. DNA is a marvel of biological data storage. The double helix structure... well, everyone knows Watson and Crick, but Rosalind Franklin and her X-ray crystallography work were absolutely essential to understanding that shape. X-ray crystallography is incredible. You shoot X-rays at a crystal, and the diffraction pattern tells you the atomic structure. \n\nX-rays are just high-frequency electromagnetic radiation, just like visible light, or radio waves. Radio waves are how we study the furthest reaches of the universe. Radio astronomy has given us so much insight into pulsars. Those are highly magnetized, rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation. They spin so precisely, you could set a clock to them. Timekeeping itself has such a rich history, from sundials to water clocks to modern atomic clocks that measure the vibration of cesium atoms...\n\nBut, oh, I apologize, I have drifted off again. You were asking about my daily functioning? Yes, I am perfectly fine in that regard. When I am not dealing with the whole situation at the apartment building, I can still manage all my finances, I cook my own meals, I keep all my appointments, and I can discuss my old consulting work or my painting in a completely organized way. The oculus at the top lets in this perfect beam of sunlight that tracks across the interior space throughout the day. \n\nTracking time using the sun is fascinating. Sundials are one of the oldest scientific instruments. I actually bought an antique brass sundial at an estate sale once, hoping to put it in the garden of my old house. The craftsmanship on the gnomon—that's the part that casts the shadow—was just exquisite. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, you know. No, nothing like that. My mind is my own.\n\nDoctor: How old were you when these beliefs and experiences first started?\n\nPatient: Well, let's see... Moving is notoriously one of the most stressful life events a person can go through, right up there with divorce or job loss. I actually read a fascinating study once on the psychology of relocation. It has to do with the disruption of our spatial memory and routine. \n\nSpatial memory is largely processed in the hippocampus, you know. That's the same part of the brain that's affected early on in Alzheimer's disease. The hippocampus is named after the Greek word for seahorse, because of its curved shape. I remember catching fireflies in a glass jar when I was a kid growing up in Ohio. We used to poke holes in the metal lid with a nail and a hammer so they could breathe. The sound a hammer makes when it strikes metal... it's a very distinct acoustic resonance. It depends on the density of the metal and the shape of the object being struck...\n\nBut, yes, to answer your question, I was 64 when I moved into the apartment and all this began, about 11 months ago.\n\nDoctor: Have you become much less interested in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Less interested? It's fascinating how environment dictates biology like that. Just like the Arctic fox, which changes its coat from brown in the summer to pure white in the winter for camouflage. Camouflage in the animal kingdom is just extraordinary. Depression or mania? No, I haven't experienced anything like that. I've certainly never been manic. Mania implies a sort of boundless, uncontrollable energy, doesn't it? 

Energy is such a fundamental concept, though. In my management consulting days, I actually did a comprehensive efficiency analysis for a regional power grid. It has to do with the disruption of our spatial memory and routine. \n\nSpatial memory is largely processed in the hippocampus, you know. That's the same part of the brain that's affected early on in Alzheimer's disease. The hippocampus is named after the Greek word for seahorse, because of its curved shape.
